findings.issue: The resolver reads only the first X-Forwarded-For field line (getHeaders().getFirst). A client can send its own X-Forwarded-For line, e.g. 'X-Forwarded-For: 6.6.6.6, 6.6.6.6'. If CloudFront or the ALB add their hop by appending a separate field line, or by appending to the last line instead of merging all lines into one, then getFirst returns only client-controlled data. The N-th entry from the right would then be forged. RFC 9110 5.3 says multiple field lines are the same as one comma-joined list, so reading only the first line is not correct. The code moved this unchanged from RateLimitWebFilter, but before this change it only chose a rate-limit bucket. Now it becomes X-Internal-Client-Ip, which slice 2 makes the trusted source for the audit IP, the wallet per-IP limit, auth login throttling and the referral IP check. Nothing in objective.md, the design or the tests shows how CloudFront or the ALB handle duplicate XFF lines. That is the same kind of unproven runtime assumption that F-20261119-01 was flagged for.
findings.fix: Build the candidate list from every XFF value in order, for example String.join(",", request.getHeaders().getOrEmpty("X-Forwarded-For")), then split and count N from the right. Add a contract-test case and an integration-test case with two XFF header lines (client line '6.6.6.6' plus a later line ending in the real entry), and assert that the key and the header both equal the real entry.

findings.issue: For bracketed input, the parser keeps the text inside the brackets and ignores everything after ']'. So '[::1]garbage' and '[1.2.3.4]:x:y' are accepted. This cannot be used for injection, because only a canonical InetAddress is ever emitted. But the parser is less strict than the 'strict literal' contract it claims to be.
findings.fix: After ']', accept only an empty remainder or ':' followed by 1-5 digits. Otherwise return empty. Add both inputs to ClientAddressTest.rejects.

findings.issue: The N-from-right rule is only safe if the gateway can be reached only through the N trusted proxies. If the ALB (or the gateway) can be reached without going through CloudFront, a client can set the entry that sits N from the right. The impact of this is now larger, because the value feeds audit, the wallet limit and the referral check, not just a rate-limit bucket. This is an existing deployment precondition that is not stated in the slice.
findings.fix: In the ADR/runbook (AC-12 doc in slice 2), state the precondition that the ALB accepts traffic only from the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list (or checks a secret origin header), and that the gateway Service is not publicly exposed. Alternatively, file it as a backlog item.

summary: I checked the slice against the attack paths you listed. Only one is still open: multiple X-Forwarded-For field lines. The other paths hold. Every client-sent x-internal-* header is stripped at the very first filter (InboundHeaderSanitizationWebFilter, order -300). The strip matches on lower-cased header names, so letter case does not matter, and it removes repeated lines too. The new header is set only by a GlobalFilter at order 1, which runs only for requests that matched a route. Requests that get 401/403/429, match no route, or hit actuator never reach it, and the integration test confirms this by counting stub hits. set() replaces any existing value, and when the address cannot be resolved the header is removed rather than left blank. No DNS lookup can happen: parsing uses InetAddress.ofLiteral, formatting uses getByAddress/getHostAddress, and the peer is read from getAddress(), which returns null for unresolved addresses. Overlong input is capped at 64 characters and parsing takes linear time. Netty's header-size limit bounds the XFF split, so I found no parsing DoS. Zone ids, brackets, v4:port, IPv4-mapped and upper-case IPv6 all reduce to one canonical form. Shorthand IPv4 such as '1' or '127.1' and hostnames now fall back to the socket peer. The change in how rate-limit keys are formatted is bounded: at worst there is a one-minute bucket reset at deploy, and it does not let an attacker split their requests across more buckets. No secrets or PII are added to logs; the strip filter logs header names only. No dependencies are added. I am requesting changes for one major issue. The resolver reads only the first X-Forwarded-For line, and nothing proves CloudFront or the ALB merge duplicate lines. Because this value is now the platform-wide trusted client IP, a client could forge it. The fix is to join all XFF values before counting from the right, and to add tests for it.
